brief.situation: Monday 09:00. You look after AWS for a small online tutoring company in us-east-2 (Ohio). Last month's bill shows about $1,810 for data transfer, against a budget of $1,000. The month before it was about $910.
handover: Learners stream and download course videos from an S3 bucket. Tutors upload about 3 TB of raw recordings a month.
Web servers run in two Availability Zones; the database runs in AZ a with a standby in AZ b. Nightly backups are copied to us-west-2 under the disaster-recovery plan.
Last quarter the platform team ran a disaster-recovery test.
howItWorks: Learner-paced: nothing moves until you act. Investigate, make changes, then run the week.
The meters show the projected monthly data transfer bill and the site's availability.
Before you run the week you are asked what drove the bill and what you changed. The debrief scores what you did.

inQ.title: Uploads
inQ.context: Tutors upload about 3 TB of recordings a month from the internet into S3. What do those uploads cost in data transfer?

choices.label: Nothing: data transfer in from the internet is free
choices.feedback: Right. Inbound transfer is $0 per GB; you pay for data going out, to the internet or to another Region, and between AZs.

choices.label: About $270, the same $0.09 per GB as downloads
choices.feedback: No. Data transfer in from the internet is free; the $0.09 is for data going out.

then.log: Tuesday: data transfer running at about {round(cost / 30)|usd} a day.
Wednesday 14:00: AWS Health reports impaired connectivity in us-east-2a for 90 minutes. The database fails over to its standby in AZ b.
Every web server is in AZ a: the site is down for 90 minutes.

else.log: The web servers in AZ b keep the site up.

then.log: Thursday: a mistaken lifecycle rule deletes this week's backups in us-east-2.
The us-west-2 copies are intact; backups restored from Oregon.

else.log: Replication was off since Monday: this week's backups exist nowhere else.

plan.question: Before you run the week: which kinds of data transfer cost money, which one drove this bill, and what did you make sure not to break?

parts.label: The charges
parts.criteria: Inbound free; outbound to the internet charged ($0.09 per GB here); Region to Region charged ($0.02 per GB to us-west-2); between AZs charged ($0.01 per GB); names the leftover replication rule as the driver.
parts.modelAnswer: Uploads coming in are free. Downloads to learners cost about $0.09 per GB, copies to us-west-2 $0.02 per GB, and traffic between AZs $0.01 per GB. The jump is 45 TB a month copied to Oregon by a replication rule left over from a DR test.

parts.label: What not to break
parts.criteria: Confirms the copy is unused before turning it off; keeps the backups' replication for disaster recovery; keeps two AZs because the cross-AZ saving is small; adds a budget alert.
parts.modelAnswer: Check with the owner, then turn off only the DR-test rule. Keep the backups copy the DR plan needs, and keep the web servers in two AZs: $60 a month is not worth an outage. Add a budget alert so the next jump shows up within a day.

expertPath.text: Cost Explorer by usage type: the jump is us-east-2 to us-west-2. Replication rules: a DR-test rule still copies raw uploads. Ask the owner: unused.
Turn off only the DR-test rule. Keep the backups copy and both AZs. Put CloudFront in front of the videos.
A budget alert at 80%, actual and forecast. The trade-off: about $100 a month of cross-AZ and backup transfer kept on purpose, for availability and recovery.

outage.headline: Site outage
outage.body: Traffic between AZs costs $0.01 per GB, about $60 a month here. Putting every server in one AZ saved that and lost the site for 90 minutes when the AZ had trouble.

dataLoss.headline: Backups lost
dataLoss.body: Region-to-Region copies cost money, but the backup copy is what disaster recovery is for. Turning off all replication saved about $40 a month and left the week's backups with nowhere to be restored from.

fixed.headline: Fixed without breaking anything
fixed.body: You found the cause with data, checked with its owner, removed only the waste and kept what availability and recovery need. That is the expert path.

partly.headline: Better, by a rougher route
partly.body: Check whether you looked at the data first, whether you asked the owner before turning the rule off, and whether the cause was removed.

time_up.headline: No decision
time_up.body: The bill keeps running while nothing changes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Data transfer has a direction and a distance. In from the internet is free. Out to the internet costs about $0.09 per GB here, Region to Region $0.02 per GB, and between AZs in one Region $0.01 per GB. Cost Explorer grouped by usage type shows which line moved: the Region-to-Region line, from a replication rule left over from a DR test. Confirm with the owner, then turn off that rule only. The backup copy and the second AZ cost a little and are what keep the business running when something fails. AWS Budgets then alerts on actual or forecast spend so the next jump is seen in a day, not on the bill.
